locators.supported_principle: Use the main verb for the intended scientific action.

locators.short_quote: Highlight the subject of each sentence.
locators.supported_principle: Inspect subject continuity and intentional topic shifts.

locators.short_quote: Identify the main subject and its verb in your sentence.
locators.supported_principle: Investigate subject–verb separation where the reader must reconstruct the main action.

sources.title: Lesson 2: Cohesion, Coherence, and Emphasis
sources.authority: Duke Graduate School institutional writing lesson.
sources.read_scope: Complete substantive lesson: definitions; Principles 1–3 and revision techniques; all displayed examples; About This Guide footer. Linked worksheet, passive-voice focus articles and dangling-modifier focus article not read.

locators.supported_principle: A recognizable premise can introduce new information and reduce backward reconstruction.

locators.short_quote: underline any pieces of new information
locators.supported_principle: Use a temporary old/new-information diagnosis on actual prose.
A citation can leave execution attribution versus method provenance unclear; name the actor where necessary.

locators.short_quote: Choose passive voice for a reason
locators.supported_principle: Active/passive selection can serve information order; no voice alone confers objectivity.

locators.short_quote: make sure each sentence in a paragraph supports the main point
locators.supported_principle: Cohesion between sentences and coherence around a paragraph point are separate checks.
